Content:
Suppose we want to evaluate the infinite geometric series
[MATH: \sum_{n = 1} ^ \infty 3 \left (\dfrac 1 4\right) ^ n.]
The sum [MATH: S_\infty] of an infinite geometric series is given by the formula
[MATH: S_{\infty} = \dfrac {\color{black}a_1} {1 - {\color{black}r}},]

Content:
where [MATH: {\color{black}r}] is the common ratio and [MATH: \color{black}a_1] is the first term. So, we need to determine [MATH: \color{black}a_1] and [MATH: \color{black}r] and then plug those values into this formula.

Content:
The first term is
[MATH: {\color{black}a_1} = 3 \left( \dfrac 1 4 \right)^1 = {\color{black}\dfrac 3 4},]
and the common ratio is
[MATH: {\color{black}r} = \dfrac {a_2}{\color{black}a_1} = \dfrac {3 \left (\dfrac 1 4 \right)^2}{3\left( \dfrac 1 4 \right)^1}= {\color{black}\dfrac 1 4}.]

Content:
So, the sum of the series is
[MATH: ∑_(n = 1)^(∞)3((1)/(4))^{n}|= (a_{1})/(1 − r); = (((3)/(4)))/((1 − (1)/(4))); = (((3)/(4)))/(((3)/(4))); = 1.]

sections.normalized_html:
Notice that the given series is a geometric series because the ratio of any two consecutive terms is constant.

The sum to infinity [MATH: S_\infty] of a geometric series is given by the formula

[MATH: S_\infty = \dfrac{a_1}{1-r}, \qquad |r| < 1,]

where [MATH: a_1] is the first term and [MATH: r] is the common ratio.

We're told that the first term is

[MATH: a_1=-2.]

The common ratio is

[MATH: r = \dfrac{a_{n+1}}{a_{n}} = -0.4.]

So, the sum of the series is

[MATH: ∑_(n = 1)^(∞)a_{n}|= (a_{1})/(1 − r); = (− 2)/(1 − (− 0.4)); = (− 2)/(1.4); = − (10)/(7).]

Notice that the given series is a geometric series because it is in the form [MATH: \displaystyle \sum ar^n.]

The sum to infinity [MATH: S_\infty] of a geometric series is given by the formula

[MATH: S_\infty = \dfrac{a_1}{1-r}, \qquad |r| < 1,]

where [MATH: a_1] is the first term and [MATH: r] is the common ratio.

The first term is [MATH: a_1 = 2(0.5)^{1} = 1.]

The common ratio is [MATH: r = \dfrac{a_2}{a_1} = \dfrac{2(0.5)^2}{2(0.5)^1} = 0.5.]

So, the sum of the series is [MATH: ∑_(n = 1)^(∞)2(0.5)^{n}|= (a_{1})/(1 − r); = (1)/(1 − 0.5); = (1)/(0.5); = 2.]

First, note that the index [MATH: n] starts from [MATH: 3.] In this case, the first term is [MATH: a_3,] and so the sum to infinity [MATH: S_\infty] of this geometric series is given by

[MATH: S_\infty = \dfrac{a_3}{1-r}, \qquad |r| < 1.]

Computing the first few terms, we get:

[MATH: a_3 = \dfrac{5}{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{2(3)} = \dfrac{5}{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{6} = 5\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{7}]

[MATH: a_4 = \dfrac{5}{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{2(4)} = \dfrac{5}{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{8} = 5\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{9}]

Therefore, the common ratio is [MATH: r = \dfrac{a_4}{a_3} = \dfrac{5\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{9}}{5\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{7}} = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{2} = \dfrac{1}{4}.]

So, the sum of the series is

[MATH: ∑_(n = 3)^(∞)(5)/(2)((1)/(2))^{2n}|= (a_{3})/(1 − r); = (5((1)/(2))^{7})/((1 − (1)/(4))); = (((5)/(128)))/(((3)/(4))); = ((5)/(128))((4)/(3)); = (5)/(3(32)); = (5)/(96).]
